The story behind an idea

The Zeigarnik effect: what is left unfinished

A waiter who remembered unpaid orders and forgot them once paid inspired this experiment.

The story goes that the psychologist Kurt Lewin noticed in a Berlin café that the waiter remembered pending orders in detail but forgot them as soon as the bill was paid. His student Bluma Zeigarnik studied it in the laboratory in 1927.

Interrupted tasks

She asked participants to carry out a series of simple tasks and interrupted some before they were finished. Afterwards, they remembered the interrupted tasks better than the completed ones. Lewin explained it as a tension that persists while the goal is still open.

Later replications have given mixed results, and the effect depends on factors such as motivation. Even so, the idea helps explain why unfinished tasks pop into our heads at odd times, and why writing down a concrete plan to resume them helps us let go.

References

  1. Zeigarnik, B. (1927). Das Behalten erledigter und unerledigter Handlungen. Psychologische Forschung, 9, 1–85.
  2. Masicampo, E. J. y Baumeister, R. F. (2011). Consider it done! Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667–683.
